This reflects the structural confounding from Section~\ref{sec:confounding}: single-facet corrections leave the uncorrected confound intact, producing invariant rank orderings (Observation~\ref{obs:ovb}). G-MFRM achieves nominally higher point-estimate rank agreement ($\tau = 0.857$, $\rho = 0.952$) over the baselines ($\tau = 0.786$), but the posterior median $\tau$ equals the baseline (0.786), with the point estimate at the distribution's upper tail. Bootstrap resampling (4{,}000 posterior draws) yields $\Delta\tau$ 95\% CI $[-0.071, 0.071]$: the ranking improvement is not statistically significant at $N = 8$, though G-MFRM almost never degrades rankings ($P(\Delta\tau \geq 0) = 0.927$). On synthetic data ($N = 50$), joint estimation significantly outperforms sequential ($\tau = 0.922$ vs.\ $0.839$, Wilcoxon $p < 0.001$), confirming that the effect is real but below detection at this sample size. The rank change---gpt-4o-mini and qwen2.5-72b swap positions---is consistent with differential contamination ($P(\theta_{\text{mini}} > \theta_{\text{qwen}}) = 0.853$, $\theta$-difference 95\% CI $[-0.227, +0.722]$).

lines: Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}

-    \item We identify and formalize, under a linear approximation to the logit link, the confounding between judge bias and benchmark contamination in LLM evaluation as an omitted variable bias problem, and show that sequential correction produces directional bias proportional to model contamination levels (Section~\ref{sec:confounding}, Figure~\ref{fig:ovb_bias}).

+    \item We identify and characterize, under a linear approximation to the logit link, the confounding between judge bias and benchmark contamination in LLM evaluation as an omitted variable bias problem, and show that sequential correction produces directional bias proportional to model contamination levels (Section~\ref{sec:confounding}, Figure~\ref{fig:ovb_bias}).

\item We propose the G-MFRM framework with formal identifiability guarantees (Propositions~\ref{prop:no_new}--\ref{prop:exposure_variation} and Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient}) and quantified error propagation bounds for the staged estimation procedure (Section~\ref{sec:method}, Table~\ref{tab:error_prop}).

\item Synthetic validation confirms that joint estimation reduces ability RMSE by 51.2\% relative to sequential estimation ($p < 10^{-6}$), with Kendall rank correlation $\tau = 0.922$ versus $\tau = 0.839$ (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).

\item On Arena-Hard with 6 LLM judges and 8 target models, G-MFRM produces the first joint diagnostic of per-model contamination susceptibility and per-judge severity, with nominally improved rank agreement ($\tau = 0.857$ vs.\ $0.786$ for all seven baselines; Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).

toolUseResult.originalFile: We identify three limitations. First, the fully crossed design requirement (Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient}, condition~i) demands that every judge scores every model on every item, limiting scalability to settings with many judges or models; extending G-MFRM to incomplete designs via structured missing data models is a direction for future work; relatedly, sparse observations per item in the current design produce elevated item-level mean-square residuals (92/176 items), though model- and judge-level fit remains acceptable. Second, Stage~2 exposure estimation relies on a reference model anchor (gpt-4-0314), and exposure estimate quality depends on the anchor remaining uncontaminated relative to the benchmark; as benchmarks age, anchor validity should be periodically re-assessed. Third, the current evaluation uses a single benchmark (Arena-Hard) with eight target models; generalization to other benchmarks (e.g., MT-Bench, WildBench) and larger model populations remains to be verified. Fourth, empirical CI coverage is 71\% (50 Monte Carlo seeds), below the 95\% nominal level, indicating moderate posterior overconfidence likely due to the HalfNormal prior's boundary constraint and NUTS tree depth saturation. Point estimates and rank orderings ($\tau = 0.857$) are unaffected, but reported CIs should be interpreted as lower bounds on true uncertainty; exploring more flexible priors or post-hoc calibration is a direction for future work.

+\section{Explicit Form of the OVB Coefficient $\gamma_n$}
+\label{app:gamma}
+Under the MFRM logistic link, a first-order Taylor expansion of Observation~\ref{obs:ovb} yields an explicit approximation for the bias coefficient $\gamma_n$:
+\begin{equation}
+\label{eq:gamma_explicit}
+\gamma_n \approx \frac{\sum_{i} w_{ni} \cdot e_i \cdot p_{ni}(1 - p_{ni})}{\sum_{i} w_{ni} \cdot p_{ni}(1 - p_{ni})},
+\end{equation}

+where $p_{ni} = \sigma(\theta_n - b_i - \bar{d})$ is the MFRM predicted probability averaged over judges and $w_{ni}$ is the effective item weight (number of judge observations for item $i$ on model $n$). Eq.~\ref{eq:gamma_explicit} is a weighted mean of the exposure values $e_i$, with weights proportional to the Fisher information $p_{ni}(1 - p_{ni})$. Items near the boundary ($p_{ni} \approx 0.5$) contribute more to the bias than items at the extremes, because the logistic link is most sensitive at these points. This approximation is accurate to first order in $(c_n \cdot e_i)$; the synthetic validation in Section~\ref{sec:confounding} ($r = 0.86$) confirms that the linear approximation captures the dominant bias structure.

lines: \begin{abstract}

-LLM-as-a-judge evaluation corrects for judge bias and benchmark contamination independently, but sequential correction produces biased model ability estimates. We formalize this failure as an omitted variable bias (OVB) problem: when judge severity and contamination effects are both present, any estimator that models one while omitting the other yields asymptotically biased ability estimates---even when the two facets are uncorrelated. We propose the Gated Many-Facet Rasch Model (G-MFRM), which jointly calibrates model ability, item difficulty, judge severity, and contamination susceptibility through staged estimation with externally anchored per-item exposure indicators. Formal identifiability analysis proves that fixing exposure externally is both necessary and sufficient for parameter separation under standard multi-judge designs. Error propagation analysis establishes a critical noise threshold $\sigma_{\mathrm{crit}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(e_i)}$ below which ability estimates degrade by less than 6\%. In synthetic experiments ($N = 50$, $I = 100$, $J = 8$), G-MFRM reduces ability RMSE by 51.2\% relative to sequential estimation ($p < 10^{-6}$). First, the fully crossed design requirement (Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient}, condition~i) demands that every judge scores every model on every item, limiting scalability to settings with many judges or models; extending G-MFRM to incomplete designs via structured missing data models is a direction for future work; relatedly, sparse observations per item in the current design produce elevated item-level mean-square residuals (92/176 items), though model- and judge-level fit remains acceptable. Fourth, empirical CI coverage is 71\% (50 Monte Carlo seeds), below the 95\% nominal level, indicating moderate posterior overconfidence likely due to the HalfNormal prior's boundary constraint and NUTS tree depth saturation. Within the Many-Facet Rasch Model (MFRM) framework \citep{linacre1989mfrm}, the complete data-generating process includes both judge severity $d_j$ and a contamination interaction $c_n \cdot e_i$. lines: Existing methods address these distortions in isolation. Judge bias corrections---CyclicJudge \citep{cyclicjudge2026}, UDA \citep{uda2026}---remove systematic inter-judge differences without modeling contamination. Contamination detection tools---ConStat \citep{constat2024}, DCR \citep{dcr2025}, LogProber \citep{logprober2024}---adjust for memorization without accounting for judge effects (see Section~\ref{sec:related_work} for detailed review). A bias-first pipeline absorbs contamination-induced score inflation into ability estimates, because the bias model attributes all residual systematic variation to genuine ability. A contamination-first pipeline misattributes judge severity differences as contamination, because score elevation from a lenient judge is indistinguishable from elevation due to memorization without a joint model. In either ordering, the first correction stage produces estimates distorted by the unmodeled facet, and the second stage inherits this distortion.

We propose the Gated Many-Facet Rasch Model (G-MFRM), which combines the multi-facet structure of MFRM \citep{linacre1989mfrm, jiao2025mfrm_llm} with the gating mechanism of Doubly-Gated Item Response Theory (DG-IRT) \citep{shu2013dgirt} to jointly estimate model ability, judge severity, and contamination susceptibility in a single measurement framework. G-MFRM extends the MFRM linear predictor with a multiplicative contamination gating term $c_n \cdot e_i$, where $c_n \geq 0$ captures model-specific contamination susceptibility and $e_i \in [0,1]$ quantifies per-item exposure. When $c_n = 0$ or $e_i = 0$, the gating term vanishes and the model reduces to standard MFRM, so uncontaminated model-item pairs incur no distortion. Because the bilinear product $c_n \cdot e_i$ cannot be uniquely decomposed from response data alone, G-MFRM employs a three-stage calibration procedure: (1) standard MFRM warm-start to obtain initial parameter estimates, (2) external per-item exposure estimation from evidence independent of the response data, and (3) joint Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling with $e_i$ fixed from Stage~2. We provide a formal identifiability analysis (Propositions~\ref{prop:no_new}--\ref{prop:exposure_variation} and Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient}) that proves fixing $e_i$ externally is both necessary and sufficient for parameter separation under standard multi-judge designs (Section~\ref{sec:method}). A complementary error propagation analysis bounds the impact of Stage~2 measurement noise: when exposure estimation error satisfies $\sigma \leq 0.2$, ability RMSE degradation remains below 6\%. Figure~\ref{fig:framework} provides an overview of the complete framework.

lines: Rather than detecting or correcting for contamination post hoc, an alternative strategy prevents it by design. LiveBench \citep{livebench2025} constructs evaluation items from frequently updated sources (e.g., recent news, newly released datasets) so that items post-date model training cutoffs. TRUCE \citep{truce2024} keeps test sets private via confidential computing, evaluating models without revealing items to model owners. These approaches are complementary to G-MFRM: contamination avoidance reduces the prevalence of exposed items, while G-MFRM corrects for residual contamination on items that have already leaked.

Bootstrap resampling (4{,}000 posterior draws) yields $\Delta\tau$ 95\% CI $[-0.071, 0.071]$: the ranking improvement is not statistically significant at $N = 8$, though G-MFRM almost never degrades rankings ($P(\Delta\tau \geq 0) = 0.927$). On synthetic data ($N = 50$), joint estimation significantly outperforms sequential ($\tau = 0.922$ vs.\ $0.839$, Wilcoxon $p < 0.001$), confirming that the effect is real but below detection at this sample size. The rank change---gpt-4o-mini and qwen2.5-72b swap positions---is consistent with differential contamination ($P(\theta_{\text{mini}} > \theta_{\text{qwen}}) = 0.853$, $\theta$-difference 95\% CI $[-0.227, +0.722]$).

These values satisfy the traditional convergence thresholds ($\hat{R} < 1.05$, ESS $> 100$; \citealp{gelman2013bda}) but do not meet the stricter criteria of \citet{vehtari2021rhat} ($\hat{R} < 1.01$, ESS $> 400$), which may contribute to the moderate posterior overconfidence observed in synthetic CI coverage (71\%; see Limitations). Posterior predictive checks confirm adequate model fit (predicted response rate $0.593$ vs.\ observed $0.599$; Appendix~\ref{app:ppc}). Contamination susceptibility $\hat{c}_n$ exhibits a significant gradient by model age. Four models have 95\% CIs entirely above 1.0: GPT-3.5-Turbo ($5.60$ [4.40, 6.80]), GPT-4-0613 ($4.20$ [3.10, 5.30]), Qwen2.5-72B ($3.00$ [1.40, 4.60]), and LLaMA-3.3-70B ($2.50$ [1.10, 3.90]). The most recent models show weak contamination with CIs near zero: GPT-4o ($0.88$ [0.05, 2.20]) and GPT-4o-mini ($0.93$ [0.06, 2.20]). The top-two and bottom-two CIs do not overlap, and the global shrinkage scale $\hat{\sigma}_c = 2.40$ [1.70, 3.40] confirms substantial inter-model heterogeneity. The mean $\bar{c} = 2.50$ aligns with the strong-contamination regime in our synthetic validation, confirming that benchmark contamination in Arena-Hard is non-negligible. Notably, sequential estimation yields near-zero contamination estimates ($\bar{c} \approx 0$), demonstrating that without joint modeling, contamination effects are entirely absorbed into ability estimates $\hat{\theta}$---precisely the omitted variable bias predicted by the theoretical analysis (Section~\ref{sec:confounding}). Judge severity $d_j$ separates by provenance: proprietary judges score more strictly (Claude Opus $+0.60$, GPT-5.5 $+0.53$, DeepSeek $+0.31$) than open-source judges (Mistral $-0.74$, LLaMA $-0.42$, Qwen2.5-72B $-0.35$). 4	\subsection{Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Data and models.} We evaluate on Arena-Hard \citep{li2024arenahard}, a benchmark of 316 multi-turn conversational items selected for high separability among frontier models. After filtering for full coverage across all judges and target models, the evaluation set contains 176 items in a fully crossed design. Eight target models spanning proprietary and open-source families are evaluated (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}). Ground-truth rankings are derived from Chatbot Arena human preference data \citep{zheng2023mtbench}.
8	
9	\paragraph{Judges.} Six LLM judges score all model responses in position-swapped pairwise mode: GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Mistral-Large-2, LLaMA-3.3-70B, and Qwen2.5-72B. Position swapping controls for position bias and doubles the effective observation count. Note that Qwen2.5-72B serves as both judge and target model, creating a self-evaluation scenario. We retain this overlap by design to test G-MFRM's robustness under self-evaluation: the $d_j$ parameter can absorb systematic self-evaluation bias, and the contamination gating term separates any memorization-driven inflation from judge-specific effects. A sensitivity analysis removing Qwen2.5-72B as judge is left to future work (see Limitations).
10	
11	\paragraph{Exposure estimation.} Per-item exposure $e_i$ is estimated via a two-source pipeline (\S\ref{sec:staged}): reference model anchoring with gpt-4-0314 as anchor (75\% weight) and cross-model agreement (25\% weight). The pipeline is robust to weight configuration (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.998$ across all configurations tested).
12	
13	\paragraph{MCMC.} We use NumPyro NUTS with 4{,}000 warmup and 4{,}000 sampling iterations across 4 chains (target acceptance 0.95). The contamination prior follows the hierarchical HalfNormal specification (Eq.~\ref{eq:contam_prior}). Convergence is assessed via rank-normalized split-$\hat{R}$ and bulk/tail ESS \citep{vehtari2021rhat}.
14	
15	\subsection{Baselines and Main Results}
16	\label{sec:main_results}
17	
18	We compare G-MFRM against seven methods that address judge bias or contamination separately: (1) Raw Average, (2) MFRM-only (Eq.~\ref{eq:mfrm}), (3) Sequential pipeline (MFRM then contamination adjustment), (4) CyclicJudge \citep{cyclicjudge2026}, (5) CyclicJudge+discard (exposed items removed), (6) DCR Factor \citep{dcr2025}, and (7) Preference Leakage calibration \citep{preference_leakage2026}. All methods are evaluated by Kendall $\tau$ and Spearman $\rho$ against Chatbot Arena human rankings.

lines: \section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

-We introduced G-MFRM, which jointly estimates model ability, judge severity, and contamination susceptibility by formalizing their confounding as omitted variable bias. On Arena-Hard, G-MFRM produces the first joint contamination--severity diagnostic, with nominally higher rank agreement ($\tau = 0.857$ vs.\ $0.786$; not significant at $N = 8$). The framework requires a multi-judge panel and externally estimated per-item exposure indicators---conditions met by standard LLM evaluation pipelines but not by single-judge or closed benchmarks. Validation on larger model populations (e.g., $N \geq 30$) would improve statistical power for detecting ranking differences and is a natural next step. Validation on larger model populations ($N \geq 30$) would improve statistical power for ranking differences.
